Colorfle answer today: how the mix should be read

The reveal card on this page shows your submitted guess next to the target color. When reviewing the match, look at the brightness and saturation first, not just the hue. A correct hue with too much brightness means you've over-weighted one of your RGB channels. Too dull? You're likely missing intensity from one channel entirely. The three input slots represent red, green, and blue values ranging from 0 to 255 each. Adding these together creates white; removing them creates darker shades. What the source colors are telling you

Each of the three input fields corresponds to a primary or secondary channel. Red alone gives pure red; red plus green (equal parts) produces yellow. Green plus blue makes cyan. All three at full strength yields white. The clue widgets on today's board break down which combinations produce common target families—warm tones lean on red and green, cool tones depend on blue mixed with either red or green.

Players who track their attempts notice patterns in how targets distribute across the three slots. Some days favor high-value inputs (150+) across all three channels, producing bright pastels. Others require stark contrasts—one channel maxed while others sit near zero—to hit muted or deeply saturated targets. The archive link lets you compare today's board against previous days to spot whether certain value ranges cluster together.

Why additive color logic beats random mixing

Randomly adjusting values hoping for a match wastes attempts. Additive mixing follows predictable rules. Each RGB channel contributes independently to the final output. If your current guess undershoots the target's green component, adding green raises the overall result toward whatever greens exist in the target. You don't need to touch red or blue unless those also miss.

This isolation technique—adjusting one channel at a time—typically resolves most mismatches within two or three tweaks. Start by identifying which channel diverges most from the target's visible character. Is the target warmer than your guess? Boost red. Cooler? Reduce it or push blue higher. Once the hue aligns, fine-tune brightness by raising or lowering all three channels proportionally.

Easy adjustment path for the next Colorfle

If you're approaching tomorrow's puzzle fresh, begin by estimating the dominant hue family. Warm targets (oranges, yellows, reds) need strong red and green contributions. Cool targets (blues, cyans, purples) rely on blue paired with either red or green depending on whether they trend warm or neutral. Neutral targets—grays, browns, whites—require balanced or selectively muted channel values.

Set your first guess to roughly equal parts across all three channels, then observe the direction of error. From there, single-channel adjustments get you the rest of the way. The hint widgets refresh daily, so checking them before your first submission often reveals whether the target leans toward saturation or desaturation. That single piece of directional guidance can shave an attempt off your solve time.

No. RGB addition is commutative—the result stays the same regardless of which slot holds which value. What matters is the numeric combination, not the sequence.

When you're uncertain, default to the physical, countable version of your idea.

Starting words heavy with English-pattern letters will miss these distributions.

The other trap is assuming Q, X, and Z are dead letters. They aren't common, but Welsh has borrowed some words that use them. J appears in loanwords. The board doesn't cheat—it plays by Welsh orthography rules, which means occasionally you'll see a K where English wouldn't expect one.
